story1004:
Wenebojo, hungry and lazy, saw a flock of geese dancing on the shore of a great lake. They moved in perfect formation, their orange feet stamping the sand, their wings spread wide, their voices rising in a beautiful song.

Wenebojo was jealous. He wanted to join their dance, not because he loved dancing but because he loved eating, and the geese looked plump.

He approached them and said, "I have seen a more beautiful dance in my dreams. Let me teach you."

The geese were suspicious. Wenebojo was known for his tricks. But he was so earnest, so apparently sincere, that they agreed to let him join their circle.

"Close your eyes," Wenebojo instructed. "The dance is more beautiful when you feel it rather than see it."

The geese closed their eyes. Wenebojo joined their circle, dancing with them, singing with them. And as they danced with their eyes shut, Wenebojo began to wring their necks — one by one, silently, efficiently.

He was halfway through the flock when a young goose opened its eyes. It saw what was happening and cried out a warning. The remaining geese flew away, their wings beating the air in panic.

Wenebojo was left with a pile of dead geese. He had enough food for many days. But his treachery was discovered, and he faced the consequences — for the spirits do not forget, and dishonesty leaves a mark that cannot be washed away.

The story teaches both humor and the lesson that dishonesty will eventually be exposed. Wenebojo's trick worked, but it cost him the trust of the geese forever.
story1005:
In the beginning, fire belonged only to the spirits. It burned in the lodge of the Old Man who guarded the flame, and the people shivered in the cold. They ate their food raw, their teeth grinding against uncooked meat. Their fingers were stiff with cold, their breath visible even in summer.

Nanabozho, the culture hero, decided to steal fire for humanity. He traveled to the lodge of the Old Man, a place of warmth and light surrounded by a garden of ice. A fierce serpent guarded the entrance, its body coiled around the doorpost, its eyes never closing.

Nanabozho transformed himself into a rabbit to sneak past the serpent. He hopped through the garden, his small body hidden by the snow. The serpent saw only a rabbit and ignored him.

Inside the lodge, Nanabozho found the fire — a living flame that pulsed with warmth. He grabbed a burning brand and fled.

The Old Man woke with a roar. The serpent uncoiled and gave chase. Nanabozho ran with the fire in his paws, the serpent hissing behind him, the Old Man's shouts shaking the trees.

As he ran, the fire scorched the trees around him, leaving black marks on their white bark. The birch trees bore these marks forever — the scars of Nanabozho's gift.

Nanabozho passed the fire to the animals, who relayed it to the people. One by one, each animal carried a burning brand from the next, creating a chain of fire that reached every village.

Ever since, the people have had fire for warmth and cooking. And the birch tree's black marks are a reminder of the night Nanabozho stole fire from the spirits and gave it to the world.
story1006:
Long ago, when Wenebojo was wandering the earth, he discovered that the maple trees produced thick, sweet syrup that flowed freely from their trunks. The sap ran in the spring, filling buckets and troughs with liquid gold.

The people had only to collect it and drink their fill. The syrup was abundant — more than anyone could drink, more than anyone could store. It was a gift from the trees, given freely.

Wenebojo, being lazy and greedy, drank so much that he became sick. His stomach heaved, his head spun, and he collapsed beneath a maple tree, sticky with the syrup he had spilled.

When he recovered, he was angry. He blamed the trees for his sickness. "You tricked me," he said. "You gave me too much."

Angrily, he threw water into the trees, diluting the sap. He took his spear and stabbed the birch tree full of holes, declaring that in the future people would have to work hard to get maple sugar.

Before Wenebojo's anger, the sap ran thick and sweet, ready to drink. After his anger, it ran thin and watery. People would have to gather forty barrels of sap to make one barrel of sugar — boiling it for hours over fires, stirring it until it thickened, working hard for what had once been free.

The birch tree still bears the marks of Wenebojo's spear — the horizontal lines that pattern its white bark. They are a reminder that even the greatest gifts can be spoiled by greed and anger.

The story teaches that the natural world gives freely, but when humans take too much or too greedily, the gifts become harder to obtain.
story1007:
Long ago, the giant lynx Mishipeshu had imprisoned all the summer birds in a cave beneath the earth. Without the birds, there was no spring song, no dawn chorus, no promise of warmth. The world lay under endless winter — snow covering everything, ice coating every branch, the wind howling without relief.

The animals held a council. They gathered in the largest den they could find, their breath steaming in the cold, their bodies thin from hunger. They discussed the problem at length. The rabbit suggested a direct assault. The bear proposed negotiation. The fox suggested trickery.

It was Fisher — small, swift, his fur the color of autumn leaves — who volunteered to lead the rescue. "I am the swiftest," he said. "I can slip past Mishipeshu while the others distract him."

The plan was simple. The larger animals — bear, moose, deer — would approach Mishipeshu's cave and make noise, drawing the giant lynx away from the entrance. Fisher would slip inside and release the birds.

The plan worked. The animals charged the cave, their hooves and paws shaking the ground. Mishipeshu emerged, his eyes blazing, his body huge enough to block the entrance. He pursued the animals across the frozen landscape.

Meanwhile, Fisher slipped inside the cave and found the birds — hundreds of them, huddled in darkness, their feathers dull with cold. He opened the cage and the birds flew out, streaming into the sky like a river of color.

Summer returned. The snow melted, the rivers ran, the grass grew green. But Mishipeshu pursued Fisher across the sky, his rage undimmed.

As Fisher ran, the spirits lifted him higher and higher into the heavens, where he was transformed into the constellation we call the Big Dipper. Every year, when the constellation appears in the northern sky, it signals the return of spring.
story1008:
The Great Horned Serpent Mishiginebig, ruler of the underwater world, had been devouring the people who lived near the Great Lakes. It rose from the water at night, its antlered head breaking the surface like an island, its eyes burning with a cold light.

Nanabozho, the culture hero, vowed to destroy the monster. He transformed himself into a tree stump on the shore and waited.

For many days he waited, motionless, patient. The waves lapped against his roots. The birds perched on his branches. The sun rose and set, and still he waited.

Finally, the serpent surfaced. Its body was enormous — as long as a canoe fleet, its scales the color of deep water. Its antlered head rose from the lake, water streaming from its jaws.

Nanabozho struck. He transformed back to his human form and hit the serpent with his magical club. The blow was tremendous — it shook the lake, sent waves crashing against the shore, scattered the birds from the trees.

The serpent fought back. Its body coiled around Nanabozho, squeezing, crushing. The waters of the lake churned into a furious storm.

But Nanabozho was stronger. He struck again and again, his club rising and falling with the rhythm of a heartbeat. The serpent weakened. Its coils loosened. Its eyes dimmed.

Finally, the serpent fell. Its body sank to the bottom of the lake, and its dying breath caused a great flood that nearly destroyed the world.

This flood led to the recreation of the earth from mud brought up by the muskrat. The story teaches the danger of disrupting the balance between the upper and lower worlds, and that even the greatest victories come with costs.
